Description: The Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine M.S. program in Anatomy Education program is designed to train students to teach anatomy and physiology at the community college and undergraduate level. It is also well-suited for students wishing to strengthen their credentials for admission to a variety of doctoral programs (including medical and dental school), as well as those interested in careers as an anatomy lab manager or curriculum specialist. The core of this one-year, full-time program is a series of courses that provide intensive immersion in human anatomy through both classroom instruction and dissection laboratories. A teaching practicum, which provides training and experience in the instructional delivery of anatomical knowledge, is also included in the program. Some exposure to nonhuman comparative anatomy is incorporated to provide training in the use of model organisms for instructional programs that use these models.

Description: The Anthropology Department specializes in socio-cultural anthropology: the study of social and cultural forms of human life using ethnographic, historical, and comparative methods. [8, 12] Department faculty are engaged in research that addresses topics considered traditional such as the study of ethnicity, language, religion, family and kinship, or medical pluralism, and also new and emergent issues such as those relating to childhood, technological imaginaries, biomedicine, ecology, state, violence, and popular economies. [8] The training of graduate students focuses on providing students with a vocabulary and grammar to engage in anthropological reasoning in socio-cultural anthropology and with skills in research methods. [8] The department emphasizes training in anthropological theory in relation to new developments in other disciplines within the social sciences; understanding of regions in terms of cross-cutting questions rather than geographical questions alone; and the capability to place a problem within a broad history of anthropology that is engaged through multiple national and regional traditions. [8] Students will usually spend three years in residence, one year or more conducting field research, and a final year completing the dissertation. [4, 13]

[3] Applicants must submit a one page personal statement indicating the basis of their interest in graduate study and their career objectives. Description: The PhD program in the History of Medicine is part of the broader Program on the History of Science, Medicine, and Technology jointly run by the Department of the History of Medicine (SOM) and the Department of the History of Science and Technology (KSAS). [2] The work of the PhD program extends over all phases and dimensions of the development of medicine and related sciences, the history of disease, and the historical analysis of related conceptual, cultural, and social problems. [2] Students acquire facility in the methods of historical research and gain a wide acquaintance with the available literature in the history of medicine, science, and related fields of history. [2] Departmental offerings are particularly strong in the history of medicine and science in early modern Europe and the Islamic world; medicine, science, and technology in the United States in the 19th and 20th centuries, including genetics; history of disease and public health; and studies of health and society in Latin America and Africa. The program offers coverage of racism and gender in the history of medicine, how medical and scientific knowledge is created, and medical practices of the body. [2] The PhD program prepares students for scholarly careers in teaching, research, and in non- academic fields. [2]

Description: The PhD in Interdisciplinary Humanistic Studies (IHS) is a new doctoral program, funded by a grant from the Mellon Foundation, that aims to facilitate the investigation of topics and problems that benefit from the insights of two disciplines. Under this program, first and second-year doctoral students have the unique opportunity to design a customized interdisciplinary PhD curriculum that they will pursue over the remaining years of their doctoral study.This D. provides students with an avenue to pursue training and research that may not be easily carried out within the framework of an established PhD, and that stands to produce novel interdisciplinary research results and innovative curricula that impact two (or more) fields at once. IHS students work with faculty advisors from two different PhD fields, combining the methods, resources, and requirements of the two fields to develop and carry out their specific interdisciplinary course of study and research. At least one of these fields must be in the humanities or humanistic social sciences.

Description: The five-year BA/MA program with the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS) in Washington, D.C., allows select undergraduate students to pursue an intensive program in international studies and also obtain a Master of Arts in International Relations (MAIR) from SAIS. [2] The BA/MA program with SAIS includes three years of study at the Homewood campus and two years of study at SAIS. [2] Formal attendance at SAIS begins in what would have been the senior year of undergraduate study (year four). [2] All students may apply to spend their first year of SAIS at SAIS Europe or the Hopkins-Nanjing Center. [2] The BA is not awarded until the end of the fourth year. [2] The program is open to sophomore International Studies and Political Science majors, and in some cases, East Asian Studies majors. [2] A GPA of 3.5 or above is normally required. [2]
ScholarshipType: Financial assistance for the fifth year is determined by SAIS and is not guaranteed. [5]

Students may also apply to be considered for a Ph.D. through the Interdisciplinary Humanities Studies program, working in Italian and another Department, such as Philosophy, Anthropology, Physics, and more. [5]
Description: The Italian PhD program at Johns Hopkins University emphasizes work in three complementary areas: literary history, close textual analysis, and theory of interpretation, with a focus on the study of evolving cultures of literacy—from manuscripts and the material history of the book to performance, ﬁlm, and emerging digital cultures. [2] Along with seminars in Italian studies, students are expected to take occasional courses outside their ﬁeld of specialization, especially in the areas of linguistic and literary theory, comparative literature, philosophy, history, art history, film and, media studies. [2] Teacher training and teaching practice are an essential part of the Italian graduate program, and supervised teaching is required of degree candidates in every year but the first and the fourth. [2]

Department: Zanvyl Krieger School of Arts and Sciences
Description: The Hebrew and Yiddish subdivision offers a PhD program in Jewish Languages and Literatures. [3] The program offers a philological, historical, and critical approach to Yiddish and Hebrew literatures. [3] The PhD program in Jewish Languages and Literatures requires all students to take at least four graduate seminars (or their equivalent) within the section of Hebrew and Yiddish courses offered by the Modern Languages and Literatures (MLL). [2] In addition, students are required to take at least four Jewish Studies courses offered outside of MLL. [2] By the end of their second year, students will have completed 12 seminars for credit. [3] If needed, students will continue to enroll in advanced language courses. [2] By the end of their first year, students will have developed - together with Professors Stahl and Spinner - a reading list to prepare for their Comprehensive Reading Exam, which will take place at the end of their third year. [2] All students must submit one qualifying paper and a brief dissertation prospectus. [3] The fourth and fifth years of the program are devoted entirely to the dissertation. [3] Professional training is an essential part of our graduate program. [2] A supervised teaching apprenticeship is required of degree candidates. [2]

Description: This 30-credit Master of Education degree offers a uniquely comprehensive, reflective approach to learning design. The program trains education leaders who can design, implement, and evaluate emerging technologies while leveraging the best research and practices to deliver effective, equitable learning experiences. [5] Through this new, 30-credit, online master's degree program, you will be equipped to lead and shape the future of educational technology and training, leveraging principles and practices from the learning sciences, instructional design, and the latest evidence-informed technology. [2] You will learn principles and practices from the learning sciences and gain hands-on skills in designing, delivering, and evaluating innovative and evidence-informed technology-supported learning experiences and pedagogies to improve learning outcomes in a wide range of settings. [5]

Department: Krieger School of Arts and Sciences
Description: The JHU Master of Liberal Arts program thrives on your curiosity, passion, and diverse world experience. The first program of its kind in the country, this educational experience allows you to pursue a graduate degree tailored to your interests, whether you're looking for an advanced credential for career mobility or simply want to enrich your personal and professional life. You'll have access to a diverse and creative selection of interdisciplinary courses each semester, with topic-driven offerings that draw from disciplines like history, film, art, music, literature, sociology, politics, world cultures, bioethics, psychology, ecology, and archaeology.

Department: Krieger School of Arts and Sciences
Description: By applying the same courses simultaneously toward the requirements for the BA and MA degrees, an advanced student can qualify for both degrees within the four-year period of undergraduate education. [2] Applicants to the program should complete the standard graduate application during their junior year and no later than April 30 of that year. [2] With the application, the applicant must supply an official copy of the current transcript and a statement of purpose. [2] The GRE exams are not required, and the graduate application fee is waived. [2] In addition, the applicant must have one member of the faculty of the Department of Mathematics submit a letter of recommendation. [2] All interested students must contact the academic program coordinator prior to applying. [2] Admission to the program is based on excellence in upper-division mathematics courses. [2] All BA and MA requirements must be completed within the traditional four-year time frame. [2] Graduate student financial support is not available for BA/MA candidates. [2]

Department: Zanvyl Krieger School of Arts and Sciences
Description: The goal of our PhD program is to train graduate students to become research mathematicians. Each year, an average of five students complete their theses and go on to exciting careers in mathematics both inside and outside of academia. Faculty research interests in the Johns Hopkins University Department of Mathematics are concentrated in several areas of pure mathematics, including analysis and geometric analysis, algebraic geometry and number theory, differential geometry, algebraic topology, category theory, and mathematical physics. The department also has an active group in data science, in collaboration with the Applied Math Department.

ProgramName: Master of Arts in Medical and Biological Illustration,
Department: School of Medicine
Description: The Medical and Biological Illustration (MBI) program offers a robust curriculum designed to prepare future leaders in the medical illustration profession. [3, 4] Accredited since 1970, the MBI program offers courses in visual communication of medicine and life-sciences as well as graduate level science courses in the School of Medicine. [3, 4] Courses are directly related to technical, biological, or medical subject matter. [3, 4] Student assignments require problem solving and individual research. [3, 4] Complete understanding of the topic is required. [3, 4] Expertise in all media communication utilized by clinicians, research scientists, health science personnel, students, patients, and the public is stressed. [3, 4] Applicants must hold a bachelor's degree with courses in premedical sciences, and be able to demonstrate art skills and experience which they obtained through instruction in the fine and applied arts. [4] Basic medical science courses will be offered by the School of Medicine. [4] Illustration and communications curriculum will be provided by the Department of Art as Applied to Medicine. [4] Students may individualize their study depending on previous training, professional interests, and career objectives. [3, 4] All degree candidates must satisfy the requirements of the University, the School of Medicine, and the Department of Art as Applied to Medicine. [3, 4]
Accredidation: The MBI program is accredited by the Commission on Accreditation of Allied Health Education Programs (CAAHEP) in cooperation with the Accreditation Review Committee for the Medical Illustrator (ARC-MI), which is a Committee of the Association of Medical Illustrators (AMI). [3, 4] Current Accreditation: 2019-2026. [3, 4]
ScholarshipType: Departmental scholarships are awarded to all students enrolled in the program and applied towards tuition fees. [9] Specific named scholarships include The Howard Bartner Scholarship for Excellence in Art as Applied to Medicine and The Elinor Widmont Bodian Scholarship in Medical Art. [9]

The program will require successful completion of a minimum of 38 credits for Master's degree and completion of a research thesis (in conjunction with one or more of the faculty). Full-time master's students will complete the program in two years.

Concentration: ['Clinical–Research track (CAMPEP track)', 'Research track (non-CAMPEP track)']
Description: Medical physicists are professionals with an MS or PhD degree, specializing in the technical and clinical aspects of diagnosis and therapy. They work alongside MDs and technologists, contributing to technical areas such as imaging, radiation therapy, and radiation safety. The Medical Physics PhD program at Johns Hopkins is a five-year, dual-track program. It offers two tracks: the Clinical–Research track (CAMPEP track) and the Research track (non-CAMPEP track). The initial two years consist of coursework, with at least 36 credits required (18 core and 18 elective), and maintaining a minimum GPA of 3.0. Students complete CAMPEP-accredited courses and conduct research projects under the guidance of their PI. They must also pass the Doctoral Board Oral (DBO) exam. In the Clinical–Research track (CAMPEP track), students prepare for the ABR Part 1 exam, whereas the Research track (non-CAMPEP track) is focused solely on research. Both tracks involve research projects under the PI and culminate in writing and defending a thesis. Upon completion, students in the Clinical–Research track (CAMPEP track) are qualified for Medical Physics residency, while those in the Research track are not. [3]
Accredidation: The program includes a CAMPEP core graduate curriculum and offers a Clinical–Research track (CAMPEP track) where students complete CAMPEP-accredited courses. [3, 4] CAMPEP stands for the Commission on Accreditation of Medical Physics Educational Programs. [3]
ScholarshipType: students receive a stipend provided by the principal investigator (PI)

Requirements: Admission to the Molecular and Cellular Biology M.S. program is selective. [2] Hopkins Biology majors and Molecular and Cellular Biology majors who have achieved a minimum overall grade point average of 3.2, and a minimum natural science grade-point average of 3.0, and have had at least two semesters of previous research experience may apply for admission during their junior or senior year. [2] Students with a GPA below the minimum requirement will be considered under special circumstances. [2] Admission decisions are made by the Molecular and Cellular Biology M.S. Program Committee, on the basis of: academic record, a written proposal for a project to be completed in the Mentored Research Program, letters of support and recommendation, an interview if required. [2]
Description:
The JHU Molecular and Cellular Biology Master's Program (BA/MS) is exclusively for Johns Hopkins University undergraduates majoring in biology or molecular and cellular biology. [2] Its purpose is to give these students advanced training to better prepare them for professional school or a career in science or medicine. [2] The program allows students to earn a master's degree in one academic year by building on their previous academic and research experience. [2] Program components include mentorship from Johns Hopkins faculty, specialized seminar coursework, leadership and teaching experience as a laboratory teaching assistant, and a significant independent research project that concludes with a written thesis and oral presentation. [2]

Admission to the program is selective and requires Hopkins Biology or Molecular and Cellular Biology majors to have a minimum overall GPA of 3.2 and a minimum natural science GPA of 3.0, along with at least two semesters of prior research experience. [3] Applications can be submitted during the junior or senior year. [3]

Program requirements include the completion of all B.A. or B.S. degree requirements, plus four additional advanced or specialized courses, with at least two at the 600-level or higher. [3] A core part of the program is the Mentored Research Program, which results in a thesis and an oral presentation evaluated by a Thesis Committee. [3] Additionally, serving as a teaching assistant for two semesters is a required part of the master's degree. [3]

Requirements: The combined degree is open only to Johns Hopkins University undergraduates majoring in Biology or Molecular and Cellular Biology. Application materials requested in the online application include: Transcripts, Curriculum Vitae (2 pages maximum), a Personal Statement (1 page maximum), and three letters of recommendation. [11]
Description: Ph.D. Neuroscience students at Johns Hopkins University engage in a program that includes lecture and laboratory courses, learning to understand and present current scientific literature, and conducting substantial original research. A key feature of the first year is a year-long Core Course that provides a comprehensive survey of current neuroscience, combining lectures with hands-on lab experience. The program starts in August with a mandatory 2-week 'Neuro Boot Camp' designed to give new students a foundational understanding of molecular biology and the computational and mathematical skills needed for neural systems analysis. Students are encouraged to rotate through up to three different labs to select one that aligns with their research interests for their Ph.D. research.

Requirements: The following 6 key elements for are required for application and ultimately for admission into the Program: a bachelor's degree from a qualified college or university; your updated CV; coursework with laboratory in inorganic & organic chemistry, general biology, with anatomy and physiology recommended; official transcripts of undergraduate grades; a minimum of three letters of recommendation; and. a one-to-two page personal statement including your research and career goals. [2]

Description: Pathology is an integrative discipline that looks simultaneously at the whole organism and its component cells, tissues, and molecules to study the causes and mechanisms of disease. It is a discipline that strives to understand the mechanisms of disease at fundamental levels, and to apply this understanding to improve management of these diseases in the aclinical setting. The Pathobiology Graduate Program provides a strong background in pathology and related basic sciences to prepare students for academic, research, teaching, and biotechnology careers. [10] Like the discipline of pathology itself, it straddles the traditional basic and clinical sciences. Research in Pathobiology is typically aimed toward the discovery of the basic mechanisms that cause disease with the goal of developing fresh insights leading to improved treatments or preventative measures. Thus, the students in the Pathobiology program are prepared for careers in the translation of basic biological principles to solve specific disease problems. [10] The Program provides students with opportunities to elucidate the mechanisms and origins of human diseases through an integrative approach emphasizing systemic processes based on molecular and cellular pathologic underpinnings. [10]

[2]
Description: The William H. Miller III Department of Philosophy offers programs and courses at the undergraduate and graduate levels. The courses cover major periods in the history of philosophy and many of the main topics of systematic investigation: epistemology, metaphysics, ethics, aesthetics, philosophy of language, mathematical logic, and philosophy of science. The graduate program is intended primarily for those planning to teach philosophy and make their own contributions to it. While the acquisition of a broad background in the history and different systematic fields of philosophy is required, students will have ample opportunity to develop their own special interests. The William H. Miller III Department of Philosophy encourages its students to take advantage of the rich resources of other departments at Johns Hopkins University. [16]

Applications will be ready for review with unofficial transcripts, but official transcripts will be required if an offer of admission is made.), GRE (optional), and a TOEFL or IELTS score (for international applicants). Description: When the Johns Hopkins University was founded in 1876, it was the first university in the United States designed as a center for research and doctoral education. Among its earliest graduate students were Josiah Royce and John Dewey; C.S. Peirce was an early faculty member. The William H. Miller III Department of Philosophy continues this tradition today, preparing graduate students to make original contributions to the field and to pursue careers in college and university teaching. [2] The primary goal of the program is the training of researchers who, through careers in academia, industry, and other arenas work to deepen our understanding of mental processes. [2] The PhD program is not for clinical training or counseling. [2] The degree is typically completed in five years. [3] Students will develop intensive knowledge and understanding of their area of concentration through advanced seminars, topical seminars, and research experience. [3]

ProgramName: Real Estate and Infrastructure (Part Time), Master of Science
Description: The Master of Science in Real Estate and Infrastructure (MSREI) part-time program is ideal for mid-career real estate professionals with industry experience. Working with academic and practitioner faculty, students develop the knowledge and skills needed to take advantage of the latest developments in this fast-changing profession. This core curriculum integrates the study of the major disciplines that influence real estate decisions: market analysis, law, investment analysis, finance, and development.

Description: The department's primary educational goal is to train first-class sociology PhDs. [2] The sociology graduate experience at Johns Hopkins is best characterized as a research apprenticeship – a careful blend of formal instruction, faculty-directed individual study, and supervised yet self-initiated research. [2] The department's small size and specific concentrations yield a personalized course of study and close relationships with faculty members and fellow graduate students. [2] The social climate is informal, and the mix of students and faculty, all drawn from a wide variety of geographic and social backgrounds, constitutes a rewarding intellectual community. [2] Students must complete the program requirements, which include a core curriculum, elective courses, a research apprenticeship, a teaching assistantship, a residency, and a dissertation. [2] While not required, students may choose a graduate concentration. [2] The Program on Global Social Change concentration focuses on cross-national, comparative research, and log-term, world scale social change. [2] The Program on Social Inequality concentration focuses on the causes and consequences of social inequality, the social processes that sustain it, and how social policies can reduce it. [2] For students looking to acquire advanced statistical knowledge and applied research skills, the department also offers a joint program with the Whiting School of Engineering's Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics. [2] Graduates of the program will earn a PhD in sociology and an MA or MSE in applied mathematics and statistics. [2]

Description: The Department of Sociology, Krieger School of Arts and Sciences, and the Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, Whiting School of Engineering, announce a joint program leading to a Ph.D. in Sociology and an M.A. or M.S.E. in Applied Mathematics and Statistics. [3] The purpose of the joint program is to offer Sociology doctoral students an opportunity to acquire advanced statistical knowledge and applied research skills. [3]

The School of Education offers part-time master's programs with a focus in Mild-to-Moderate Disabilities, which can lead to teacher certification, and programs with a focus in Severe Disabilities (with an emphasis on Autism Spectrum Disorders or Applied Behavior Analysis) which do not lead to teacher certification. All face-to-face classes are offered at the JHU Applied Physics Lab in Laurel, Maryland. [2]

Description: The Master of Education (MEd) for Teaching Professionals, or TeachingWell, is a teacher preparation program that a provides participants with evidence-based training while placed in partnership schools and four years of strategic support for career development and long-term success in the teaching profession. In exchange for full-tuition support while enrolled in the MEd TeachingWell program, students sign a letter of intent to apply and enter the employment of a JHU-approved Maryland school district partner for four years after completing the master's degree program. [2, 3] Developed by Johns Hopkins to address the teacher shortage and the needs of Johns Hopkins school district partners in Maryland, TeachingWell is focused on creating a diverse corps of master teachers equipped with skills and expertise in middle and high school STEM instruction and culturally responsive teaching methods. [2, 3] Environmental issues are emphasized throughout the program so that candidates can prepare students in pressing interdisciplinary STEM issues like climate change. [2] Through the unique TeachingWell residency model, students earn the MEd while gaining real-world experience in a classroom as part of a tight-knit cohort focused on ongoing mentoring, life design, social and emotional learning, and teacher wellness. [2, 3] Program goals include preparing teachers to develop expertise in content, curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, and technology; to serve as models for social justice and advocates for inclusivity and equity; and to engage in continuous learning informed by evidence from research, practice, and reflection. [3]

Description: The Center for Africana Studies in the Krieger School of Arts and Sciences pursues broad inquiry into the ideas and experiences of African peoples throughout the world. Its interdisciplinary approach is organized around three major sub-fields: African Diaspora, African-American Studies, and African Studies. [7] A major or minor in Africana Studies introduces you to the comprehensive study of the African Diaspora. [7] Our curriculum is designed to give you a unique perspective on racism, colonialism, capitalism, and geography that properly situates the importance of people of color in the making of the modern world. [6] The department particularly focuses on the challenges of our own moment in history: new religious practices and religious strife, globalization and competition, law and the problems of governance, new diseases and medical interventions, global social movements and transnational media forms, environmental crises such as climate change, and further challenges offered up by turbulence and destitution. [6, 9] Undergraduates in anthropology acquire a foundation for careers in medicine, international relations, and law, as well as preparation for graduate work in anthropology and related disciplines in the humanities and social sciences. You'll gain a solid mathematical foundation through discrete mathematics, optimization, probability, statistics, and differential equations. We also allow students the flexibility to explore other disciplines, including ones in which mathematics plays a critical role, such as biology, biomedical engineering, finance, and economics. An undergraduate major in applied mathematics and statistics takes an individually tailored program of courses within the department and in the Department of Mathematics (calculus, and perhaps further courses such as differential equations, analysis, complex variables, topology, and modern algebra) and electives in science and engineering. By suitable choice of electives, heavy concentration in a specific field of engineering is possible.

[2] The Bachelor of Science in Applied Mathematics and Statistics requires 120 credits to complete. [2] Graduates have pursued careers in various fields including the actuarial profession, financial analysis, operations research and consulting, biostatistics, information security, and data analysis, among others. [2]

The program aims to equip students with the basic skills for understanding theory, interpretation, and methods in archaeology, and to develop their ability to analyze archaeological data. Students will learn to conduct analyses and interpretations of material culture in precise, well-organized, and persuasive language, both orally and in writing. A key component of the program is gaining on-site experience and expertise in archaeological methods through fieldwork.

[12] From neuroscience labs to animal behavior to human sexuality, this interdisciplinary program allows students to explore many aspects of the biology of behavior. [12] The core program provides background and breadth in the life sciences (e.g., animal behavior, evolution), the natural sciences (e.g., biology and chemistry), mathematics (e.g., calculus and statistics), and the social and behavioral sciences (e.g., psychology and anthropology). [9] The interdisciplinary characteristics of the program provide an excellent preparation for post-graduate work, including for those interested in health professions or scientific careers in psychopharmacology, behavioral neuroscience, and physiological psychology. [7]

Description:
What is Public Health?
Public health spans several disciplines dedicated to the improvement of the health and well-being of populations across the globe. This mission broadly focuses on the prevention of illness, disease, and health care inequalities. Core disciplines include epidemiology, environmental health sciences, health policy and management, biostatistics, and social and behavioral aspects of health. These disciplines draw on a fundamental knowledge of biology, a basic familiarity with social sciences, and an appreciation of socio-economic and cultural variance among different peoples.

The Public Health Studies Major
The Johns Hopkins Undergraduate Program in Public Health is one of the first and best-known programs of its kind, and has quickly grown into the most popular major in the Krieger School of Arts and Sciences. The program offers a Bachelor of Arts degree, as well as a BA/Master’s degree in collaboration with the Bloomberg School of Public Health. A key component of the program is the applied experience requirement, which gives students the opportunity to work in the field with public health professionals. Students receive practical public health exposure and mentoring in clinical, research, or community settings.

Description: What does it take for people to engage productively as informed, skilled, and effective members of democratic communities and the world? Whether people are scientists, doctors, engineers, advocates, public servants, or anything else, they ars are scientists, doctors, engineers, advocates, public servants, or anything else, they ares of pluralistic communities. In all of these communities, people of all kinds need capacities to engage productively with one another, develop the skills to negotiate difference, and cooperate to achieve common goals. It is an applied and interdisciplinary field, incorporating critical reflection, ethical thinking, empirical understanding, historical perspectives, and action for social change within and between societies. Description: The Peabody at Homewood Program oversees music classes and the music minor on the Homewood campus of Johns Hopkins University. ProgramName: Minor in Space Science and Engineering
Description: Students seeking a minor in space science and engineering take five courses: Introduction to Space Science and Technology 171.321, plus four additional courses that are chosen by the student and approved by an adviser. [3] Students are required to submit a proposal and course plan to their adviser early in their program, prior to taking the courses. [3] The proposal must discuss a theme that unites the individual elements of the program (courses and internship(s)) into an intellectual whole. [1] The minor in space science and engineering also carries an internship (or equivalent experience) requirement. [3] Practical experience in space science and space engineering can be obtained through an academic or non-academic internship of at least six weeks of full-time effort or an equivalent duration. [2]

ProgramName: Minor in Spanish for the Professions
Department: Zanvyl Krieger School of Arts and Sciences
Description: The Spanish section offers two minors: Spanish language and Hispanic culture, and Spanish for the professions. [2] This minor offers technical courses, such as Spanish for International Commerce, Medical Spanish, Spanish for International Relations, Spanish for Engineering, Spanish for Public Health, and Spanish Translation for the Professions. [8] You'll gain a truly immersive experience through internship opportunities, where you'll receive credit for work done outside the university through the Community Based Learning–Spanish Language Practicum course, and opportunities to study abroad and do research. [8] The minor requirements consist of six (6) courses beyond the 210.212 Intermediate level. [2]

ProgramName: Minor in Theatre Arts and Studies
Department: Zanvyl Krieger School of Arts and Sciences
Fees: Tuition for a minor is included in the full-time undergraduate tuition. For the 2025-2026 academic year, an undergraduate course is listed at $6,670. [4]
Description: JHU Theatre offers a conservatory-style approach to the study of acting, directing, playwriting, and theatre history, along with the fundamentals of technical direction, play production, play analysis, and theatre management. Courses are taught by theatre professionals with practical experience in the best professional and regional theatres. Coursework is complemented by regular performance opportunities in the John Astin Theatre in Merrick Barn. The mainstage productions each fall and spring are professionally directed and designed. Each season also includes experimental performances and readings, as well as student-created performances as part of The Playshop series. For those students who seek a career in the theatre, the minor in Theatre Arts and Studies offers an introductory acting sequence, advanced classes in acting, courses in design and technical theatre, directing workshops, courses in theatre history and theory, playwriting, and independent study opportunities. The department's conservatory-style approach, with its personal attention and focus on practical training, as well as numerous opportunities for high-level performance, will provide rigorous preparation for a professional career. For those students who love theatre but are not focused on a career, JHU Theatre is an ideal component of the liberal arts. Coursework builds broad perspectives on performance and literary traditions, and it deepens an appreciation for the arts, whether theatrical, literary, musical, or visual. Play-making in Merrick Barn, whether as an actor or as part of the production team, advances skills in communication and collaboration, and brings creativity to other endeavors. Students pursuing careers in medicine, engineering, law, science, and many other areas, have been challenged and enriched by their time with JHU Theatre.

Description: Students minoring in visual arts at Johns Hopkins University can focus on studio art, fiber art, digital & analog photography courses, or a combination of two tracks. [2] The curriculum includes a diverse range of courses such as drawing, painting, mixed-media, fibers, jewelry & small metals, silkscreen and relief printmaking, digital and analog photography, and visual communication/graphic design. [6] The program is housed within the Center for Visual Arts (CVA), which engages students in innovative thinking and creative problem-solving. [8] The CVA challenges students to develop unique perspectives and take risks to push the boundaries of traditional art forms. [8] The minor requires the completion of five 3-credit or equivalent visual arts courses, along with one 3-credit art history course. [2, 3] A foundation class in drawing, oil painting, fiber, or digital photography is also required. [2, 3] At least three of the required courses must be taken through the Center for Visual Arts program at JHU, but students also have the opportunity to take courses at affiliated institutions like the Maryland Institute College of Art (MICA) or through approved study abroad programs. [2, 3]

ProgramName: Minor in Women, Gender, and Sexuality
Requirements: Students can receive a minor in women, gender, and sexuality by completing six one-semester courses. Students are asked to complete at least two courses from the core WGS curriculum and may choose among the courses cross-listed with other departments for the remaining four. [2]
Description: The WGSS interdisciplinary minor complements and may also integrate with a student's major. Students pursuing the minor in Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies take a total of six courses, including two interdisciplinary courses offered by the program and three electives from at least two different departments or programs that engage particular subjects, issues, and materials in the study of women, gender, and/or sexuality. [3] Through both interdisciplinary and specialized courses, students are encouraged to develop critical and comparative approaches to the study of gender and sexuality—often in interaction with related issues such as race, class, global health, and violence. [5]

Study in the Writing Seminars offers students the chance to engage deeply with literature, not only as readers but as writers of their own creative work. [1] The Writing Seminars department offers survey courses, workshops, readings classes, and opportunities to engage in community-based learning. [1] In addition to core classes taught every semester, recent offerings have included “Race, Passing, and Performance,” “Writing the Fantastical,” “Writing for Children and Adolescents,” “Shakespeare and Modern Poetry,” “Podcasting: Telling Stories Through Sound” and “Science and Storytelling.” [1] The minor consists of four core courses and three electives.
